newsitem.title: GERMANY: German RTL pressures CLT/Ufa over network talks.
newsitem.headline: German RTL pressures CLT/Ufa over network talks.

text.p: Germany's popular RTL television channel on Thursday reported a big jump in 1996 profit and leaned on its owner, the CLT/Ufa broadcasting group, to quickly conclude talks about setting up an RTL network.

Net advertising revenue rose 4.7 percent to 2.05 billion marksRTL ($1.2 billion) last year and net profit surged 40 percent to 144.1 million marks as the company retained its position as Germany's leading television channel in viewer ratings and ad sales.

Following the merger of Cie Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion (CLT) and the Ufa television unit of Bertelsmann AG this year, talks have been underway over creating a network in Germany made up of RTL, and the smaller RTL2 and Super RTL.

But talks have dragged on without conclusion and RTL chief Helmut Thoma, apparently frustrated, told a news conference that it was time for CLT/Ufa to make a move or else run the risk of falling behind rival Bavarian media magnate Leo Kirch.
"We hope for a return to reason. Otherwise we will have to create our own network, but I expect that talks will be concluded successfully," Thoma told reporters in Cologne.
He added that RTL was working intensively on a plan to create an independent network that would include a channel for family-oriented programming.
RTL news programming chief Hans Mahr said earlier plans to create an all-news channel were "put on ice for economic reasons".
RTL, the TV channel with the largest advertising revenue in Europe, dwarfs its two sister stations in Germany but would like to use the two channels as an outlet for surplus programming and reruns.

Thoma has often complained that while Kirch through his own shareholdings and those of his son is able to influence the programming of several stations such as Pro7, Kabel1 and Sat1, RTL does not have the same programming flexibility.
Talks about setting up an RTL network are thought to be stuck over differences over the price that CLT/Ufa would need to pay other shareholders in RTL2 and Super RTL.
Thoma said RTL has led the German television market in ratings since 1993 and ranks as Europe's leader in advertising income.

The station's average viewer ratings in 1996 totalled 17 percent, clearly ahead of public broadcasters ARD and ZDF, and its main commercial rival Sat1, which posted 14.8 percent, 14.4 percent and 13.2 percent respectively.

Thoma said RTL's 1996 profit boost was exceptional because public broadcasters had an edge with rights to show both European soccer championships and the Olympic Games, big audience-getters that attract huge advertising revenues.
Commenting on plans by rival broadcaster Pro7 to list shares on the stock exchange this year, Thoma said that RTL would be a prime candidate for a listing.
"But that is not the policy of our shareholders and we have to accept that," he said.

Separately, the German subsidiary of Nielsen, a unit of Dun and Bradstreet, said German commmercial television stations reported 8.3 percent growth in net advertising revenue in the first quarter of 1997.
A German court in Hamburg also announced that it would make a final decision on May 15 about an injuction forced by pay TV channel Premiere against its rival DF1, Kirch's digital TV broadcaster.
The injunction, which forbids DF1 from advertising or signing up customers outside of Bavaria, was temporarily lifted pending a final decision by the Hamburg court.
